an.d.panelPct: How much sunlight the configured panel captures, compared with a panel always pointed at the Sun.
an.d.tiltLossPct: How much energy is lost if the lander lands tilted (average over the directions it may tip).
an.d.tiltEarthPct: With a tilted lander, how much of the time Earth stays above the deck for the antenna.
an.d.slopeLightPct: How much light reaches a slope compared with flat ground. A slope facing away from the Sun stays dark.
an.d.reliefLossPct: Of the hours with Sun, how many the real terrain (mountains, crater rims) hides.
an.d.horizonMaxDeg: The highest mountain on the site's horizon. At the pole the Sun is low, so a few degrees already cast shadow.
an.d.tempMeanC: Estimated mean surface temperature. At the pole, with grazing Sun, it is very cold.
an.d.coldPct: Share of time below −150 °C, cold enough to damage batteries and electronics.
an.d.earthPct: Share of time Earth is above the antenna mask, so data can be sent.
an.d.blackoutH: The longest stretch without seeing Earth, with no direct communication.
an.d.powerKw: Mean power generated by the configured solar panel over the period.
an.d.lightRunH: The longest continuous sunlight: useful time to operate on solar power.
an.d.darkRunH: The longest night: how long the mission must survive without Sun.
an.d.sunEarthPct: Share of time with Sun and Earth together: generate power and transmit at once.
an.d.shadowM: Mean length of the lander's own shadow. Low Sun = long shadows that confuse cameras and sensors.
an.dn.panelPct: Right now, how much light the panel captures. No Sun = 0 and red.
an.dn.tiltLossPct: Right now, how much energy is lost with a tilted lander.
an.dn.tiltEarthPct: Right now, in how many tip directions the antenna still sees Earth.
an.dn.slopeLightPct: Right now, light on the slope compared with flat ground.
an.dn.reliefLossPct: 100% = the Sun is above the smooth horizon but hidden behind terrain right now.
an.dn.horizonMaxDeg: The highest mountain on the site's horizon (does not change with time).
an.dn.tempMeanC: Estimated surface temperature at this instant.
an.dn.earthPct: How many degrees Earth is above the horizon now. Negative = below, no contact.
an.dn.blackoutH: How many hours of contact with Earth remain. 0 = no contact now.
an.dn.powerKw: Power generated now as % of the panel maximum. Sunset → drops to 0 → red.
an.dn.lightRunH: How many hours of Sun remain before sunset. 0 = already night.
an.dn.darkRunH: If it is night, how many hours until sunrise. 0 = it is day.
an.dn.sunEarthPct: 100% = Sun and Earth are both visible right now.
an.dn.shadowM: Length of the lander's shadow at this instant.
an.h.panels: How it is computed: the Sun position seen from the site (Horizons) and the panel orientation (Solar panel card) give the angle of the rays on the panel. Why it matters: a badly oriented panel generates little power. Reference mission: SLIM (JAXA, 2024) landed with its panels facing west and only generated power again days later, when the Sun changed direction.
an.h.moduleTilt: How it is computed: the app tilts the lander X° (Simulation slider) in 8 possible directions and recomputes the light on the panel and Earth above the deck, with the real Sun and Earth. Why it matters: a tilted lander points panels and antenna badly. Reference missions: IM-1 Odysseus (2024) tipped over and struggled to point its antenna; IM-2 Athena (2025) landed on its side and its battery did not recharge.
an.h.slope: How it is computed: a slope of X° facing the chosen direction receives the rays at another angle; the app compares it with flat ground. Why it matters: slopes facing away from the Sun stay dark and cold; steep slopes are also dangerous for landing. Reference: Artemis candidate regions were chosen partly by slope and lighting.
an.h.relief: How it is computed: real horizon profile up to 150 km (Cesium Moon terrain, LOLA/NASA data) compared with the Sun position from Horizons. Why it matters: at the pole the Sun passes a few degrees above the horizon, and a crater rim already casts shadow. Reference mission: IM-2 Athena (2025) landed inside a crater on Mons Mouton, in shadow and cold, and operated only ~12 h.
an.h.temperature: How it is computed: radiative balance of the surface with the Sun elevation and distance (Horizons); at night, a floor that drops with latitude. It is an estimate, not a measurement. Why it matters: extreme cold drains batteries and damages electronics. Reference mission: IM-2 Athena, in the cold crater.
an.h.libration: How it is computed: Earth position seen from the site (Horizons), including libration, the apparent wobble of the Moon that makes Earth rise and sink in the sky. The antenna mask sets the minimum useful elevation. Why it matters: without Earth in the sky there is no direct communication; a low Earth reflects off terrain and loses signal (NASA). Reference: VIPER plans for ~2 weeks per month without seeing Earth.
an.h.power: How it is computed: solar irradiance (1361 W/m² corrected by the Horizons distance) × area × efficiency × angle on the panel. Why it matters: power keeps the mission alive.
an.h.lightRun: How it is computed: the longest run of hours with the Sun above the horizon. Why it matters: it is the useful time to operate on solar power. Reference: Blue Ghost 1 (2025) had 346 h of light and succeeded.
an.h.night: How it is computed: the longest run of hours without Sun. Why it matters: the mission needs batteries and heating to survive. Reference: VIPER was designed to survive up to ~50 h in darkness.
an.h.sunEarth: How it is computed: hours when the Sun and Earth are visible at the same time. Why it matters: that is when you can generate power and transmit data together — the core of the missions' problem.
an.h.shadow: How it is computed: lander height divided by the tangent of the Sun elevation. Why it matters: with a low Sun, shadows are dozens of times longer than the lander and fool cameras and sensors during landing. Reference: during Athena's landing, unexpected shadows hindered terrain recognition (check the NASA report).

tour.globe.title: Welcome to ViaLunae
tour.globe.text: This is the Moon in 3D, with the Sun in its real position computed by NASA (Horizons API). Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. ViaLunae helps choose where and when to land: with light for the panels, out of terrain shadow and seeing Earth to talk to it.
tour.sites.title: Landing sites
tour.sites.text: The dots on the globe are the 6 Apollo landings and 2 recent south-pole missions (IM-1 and IM-2). Click a dot to open the mission card with photos and what went right or wrong. Use "South pole" and "Global view" to navigate.
tour.scenario.title: Build a scenario
tour.scenario.text: Pick a site (or a free coordinate), the date and duration, and click "Load scenario". You see how long there is Sun, when Earth is visible, the panel's power, and you can use "Ground view" to see the real horizon.
tour.time.title: Timeline
tour.time.text: Drag the bar or press ▶ to watch the period go by: the Sun moves, the globe lighting changes and the site conditions follow.
tour.filters.title: Filters on the Moon
tour.filters.text: Tick "Show on the Moon" to paint the Moon green, yellow and red. Each filter is a real mission problem (power, terrain and shadows, communication, time). In "Now" mode the colors change with the timeline. The "?" button explains each filter.
tour.compare.title: Compare and export
tour.compare.text: Add scenarios to the comparison to see sites and dates side by side, sort by the best option and export a CSV spreadsheet. You can replay this tour with the "Tour" button at the top.
hint.label: What is this?
hint.sunNow: Sun elevation above the horizon at the start of the period. Negative = below the horizon (night). With terrain, the Sun can be above the smooth horizon yet hidden by a mountain.
hint.sunElev: The lowest, mean and highest Sun elevation in the period. At the south pole the Sun always stays low, a few degrees above the horizon.
hint.sunlight: Share of the period with the Sun visible at the site. That is when the solar panel can generate power.
hint.sunLongest: The longest continuous stretch of sunlight. It tells how long the mission can run on solar power alone.
hint.sunNext: Time until the next sunset (if it is day) or sunrise (if it is night), from the start of the period.
hint.earthNow: Earth elevation above the horizon at the start. Seen from the Moon, Earth barely moves in the sky; it only wobbles a little (libration).
hint.earthWindow: Share of the period with Earth visible: only then can data go straight to antennas on Earth.
hint.earthWindows: How many times Earth appears and disappears in the period, and the longest continuous contact window.
hint.earthNext: Time until Earth disappears (if visible) or appears (if not).
hint.delay: Time a radio signal takes from the Moon to Earth at the speed of light (about 1.3 s).
hint.powerNow: Power of the configured solar panel at the start of the period. Zero with no Sun.
hint.powerMean: Mean power over the period, counting hours without Sun as zero.
hint.powerPeak: The highest power the panel reaches in the period.
hint.energy: Total energy generated in the period (power × time). Helps size batteries and equipment.
hint.dayNight: Day: the Sun is visible. Night: the Sun is below the horizon. Terrain shadow: the Sun is above the smooth horizon but hidden by mountains or crater rims.
hint.hzSun: Height of the real terrain in the direction of the Sun at this instant. If the Sun is below this value, the site is in shadow.
hint.azEl: Azimuth: direction on the horizon, counted from north (90° = east, 180° = south). Elevation: height above the horizon.
hint.irrNormal: Solar energy reaching a surface facing the Sun (no atmosphere, about 1361 W/m²). It varies a little with the distance to the Sun.
hint.irrGround: Solar energy reaching flat ground. With a low Sun, light arrives at a steep slant and the ground receives little.
hint.temp: ESTIMATED surface temperature from the balance between absorbed light and radiated heat. At night it drops to about −170 to −220 °C. Not a measurement.
hint.earthSky: Where Earth is in the site's sky (direction and height) and whether it is above the horizon.
hint.earthPhase: How much of Earth looks lit as seen from the Moon (like Moon phases seen from Earth, in reverse).
hint.dayLength: Length of the lunar day at this site: at the equator, about 14.8 Earth days of continuous sunlight.
hint.nightLength: Length of the lunar night at this site: at the equator, about 14.8 Earth days without Sun. The hardest part to survive.
sp.title: Why is the south pole hard?
sp.intro: The south pole has water ice and peaks with lots of light, so it is the target of the next missions (Artemis, VIPER). But three things make landing and operating there hard:
sp.sun.title: ☀ Grazing Sun
sp.sun.text: At the pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees above the horizon and circles the sky over the month. Light arrives almost flat: panels must stand upright and turn, the ground gets little energy and any object casts shadows dozens of times its size.
sp.sun.mission: On Athena (IM-2, 2025), unexpected shadows hindered terrain recognition during landing (check the NASA report). On SLIM (JAXA, 2024), panels facing the wrong way left the probe without power.
sp.crater.title: ⛰ Craters in shadow
sp.crater.text: With the Sun so low, crater rims and mountains tens of kilometres away already block the light. Some crater floors never see the Sun (permanent shadow) and are extremely cold — that is where the ice is, but solar panels do not work there.
sp.crater.mission: Athena (IM-2) landed on its side inside a crater on Mons Mouton: in shadow and cold, its battery did not recharge and the mission lasted about 12 h instead of 10 days.
sp.earth.title: 🌍 Earth low in the sky
sp.earth.text: From the pole, Earth sits near the horizon and, with libration, rises and sinks a few degrees over the month. Part of the time it hides below the horizon or behind a mountain; when low, the signal reflects off the terrain and degrades.
sp.earth.mission: Odysseus (IM-1, 2024) tipped over and struggled to point its antenna at Earth. VIPER plans for about 2 weeks per month without seeing Earth.
ms.distance.hint: Click points on the Moon to measure distance along the surface. Right-click undoes the last point. Esc closes.
ms.profile.hint: Click the start and end (or more points) to see the elevation profile of the real terrain. Needs the "Cesium Moon (terrain)" surface.
ms.area.hint: Click 3 or more points to draw a polygon and see its area. Right-click undoes the last point.
ms.slope.hint: Click a point to measure the real ground slope on the Cesium Moon terrain (LOLA data).
ms.distanceNote: Measured along the surface of the lunar sphere (radius 1737.4 km), not counting ups and downs.
ms.needTerrain: Profile and slope use the 3D terrain. Switch the surface to "Cesium Moon (terrain)" (turn off the filter map and science layers, which use the flat image).
ms.error: Could not read the terrain here. Zoom in and try again.
ms.profileStats: Elevation from {min} to {max} km · total ascent {up} m · total descent {down} m · max slope {slope}°
ms.profileNote: Elevation relative to the Moon's mean radius, on the Cesium Moon terrain (LOLA). Accuracy depends on the loaded terrain detail.
ms.slopeDetail: The ground goes down toward {dir} (azimuth {az}°) · elevation {h} m · {lat}°, {lon}°
ms.slopeNote: Computed from terrain heights {m} m to each side (a baseline similar to LOLA's). Landings usually require less than 10° to 15°.
ly.title: Science layers
ly.intro: Maps measured by NASA probes, for viewing only (not used by the filters). With a layer on, the surface switches to the flat image (Moon Trek).
ly.slope.name: Terrain slope (LOLA)
ly.slope.legend: Blue = flat · green = moderate · yellow/red = steep. Coarse resolution: for one point, use the ∠ Slope tool.
ly.rocks.name: Rock abundance (Diviner)
ly.rocks.legend: Blue = few surface rocks · green/yellow/red = more rocks (young craters). Measured by the heat rocks keep at night.
ly.temp.name: Mean surface temperature (Diviner)
ly.psr.name: Permanent shadow (LOLA)
ly.psr.legend: Purple outlines: south-pole craters that never see sunlight. That is where ice may be.
ly.illum.name: Mean illumination % (LROC)
ly.illum.legend: White = lit almost always · black = almost never. Only between 88° and 90° latitude.
ly.ice.name: Stable ice (Diviner)
ly.ice.legend: Colors show how deep water ice can survive today (stronger = closer to the surface).
ly.tempPolar.name: Polar summer temperature (Diviner)
ly.tempPolar.legend: Blue = very cold · red = warmer. Shows the coldest polar craters.
tour.measure.title: Measure and view layers
tour.measure.text: Use 📏 Distance, 📈 Profile, ⬠ Area and ∠ Slope to measure right on the Moon. In the panel, "Science layers" shows maps measured by NASA: slope, rocks, temperature, permanent shadow and ice.
